items.title: Province fast-tracks northern Ont. gold mine project
items.description: A major mining investment could be on the horizon for the Matheson area, with a proposed $450 million open-pit gold mine expected to create hundreds of jobs and bring significant economic opportunities to the region.

items._ogDesc: A major mining investment could be on the horizon for the Matheson area, with a proposed $450 million open-pit gold mine expected to create hundreds of jobs and bring significant economic opportunities to the region.
items.body:
A major mining investment could be on the horizon for the Matheson area, with a proposed $450 million open-pit gold mine expected to create hundreds of jobs and bring significant economic opportunities to the region.

Mayfair Gold’s Fenn-Gib Gold Project, located 17 kilometres east of Matheson, has been designated under the provincial government’s One Project, One Process framework.

The project would include an open pit mine and an on-site mill. The province said the designation is part of its efforts to make Ontario more attractive to mining investment by streamlining the approvals process.

Ontario Minister of Energy and Mines Stephen Lecce said the initiative is intended to significantly reduce permitting timelines.

“We are, as you know, really helping to reshape the paradigm of speed by bringing forth one project, one process that is helping to really accelerate the permit timelines, cut them by half because we were among the slowest,” said Lecce.

“Today, we are among the fastest.”

For Mayfair Gold, the designation could provide a more predictable path toward construction.

CEO Drew Anwyll said the project is now looking at a permitting timeline of 18 to 24 months.

“So that’s huge, and what this really allows is improved certainty in that time frame,” Anwyll said.

The company is also hoping to take advantage of the region’s established mining workforce and network of local contractors.

Anwyll said the project is expected to create 250 permanent, long-term jobs once operational, along with another 450 jobs during construction.

“I’m keen on having as much local as we can,” said Anwyll.

“Now, what percentage is that? I don’t know just yet. But certainly, that’s the key thing. We’ll bring in as many folks as we can.”

For the Town of Black River-Matheson, the potential investment represents an opportunity for economic growth and community development.

Mayor Dave Dyment said the project could have a significant positive impact on the municipality and surrounding region.

“The opportunities for us are tremendous,” Dyment said.

“Not only are we talking jobs, but … our economy will be affected in a positive way. It’s going to give us opportunities for growth and development within our community and within our region.”

However, the mayor said preparing for that growth will also come with challenges.

“Housing would be the first one,” he said.

“Obviously, there’s going to be a great need for housing … I know we have the individuals in place to make this happen and Mayfair is working along with us all the way.”

The proposed mine will also require continued engagement with Indigenous communities in the area.

“With Abitibi, we want them to be partners. We want our success to be their success,” said Anwyll.

The company said discussions are ongoing, with a formal impact benefit agreement identified as an important next step.

Engineering and permitting work will continue through 2028, with production targeted to begin in 2030.

items.title: Apple beats sales and profit expectations but AI costs weigh on holiday sales
items.description: Apple exceeded analysts’ expectations for its latest results on Monday when the iPhone-maker said it recorded “revenue record” for a September quarter, driven by iPhone sales and services revenue.

items._ogDesc: Apple exceeded analysts’ expectations for its latest results on Monday when the iPhone-maker said it recorded “revenue record” for a September quarter, driven by iPhone sales and services revenue.
items.body:
Apple exceeded analysts’ expectations for its latest results on Monday when the iPhone-maker said it notched a “revenue record” for the July-September quarter, driven by iPhone sales and services revenue, but increased costs related to AI will drag down margins.

“We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September, said in a statement before speaking on a call with analysts Monday afternoon.

Ternus hinted at an optimistic outlook for sales of its latest products, including the foldable Duo, during the holiday season.

However, CFO Kevan Parekh warned that the company Apple’s gross marin will slow a bit in the final stretch of the year, compared to its September quarter margin of 47.9 percent.

“We expect gross margin to be between 45 percent and 46 percent. This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI,” Parekh said.

In June, the company overhauled Siri, its digital assistant, through a partnership with Google, whose Gemini model was used to beef up the new Siri AI.

Apple tried to assuage investors’ concerns about rising AI costs.

“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities,” Parekh said.

Apple launched three new phones in September -- the 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and its first folding phone called the Duo -- in addition to two new desktop computers.

In October, it also unveiled a new smart display powered by Siri AI called HomeView, as well as a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen for the first time.

In July, the company also launched Apple Upgrade, a leasing program that lets US customers pay for an iPhone or other devices in monthly installments.

Chips crunch

Long criticized for falling behind in the AI race, Apple stands to benefit from the heavy spending of its peers on data centres while keeping its own investments lean.

Analysts expected the Cupertino giant to spend US$11 billion in the 12 months that ended in September, when its fiscal year ends.

That’s a fraction of the annual expenditures of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, which are on track to spend more than $700 billion on capital investment this year -- roughly the size of Argentina’s or Belgium’s entire economy -- much of it on AI infrastructure, according to analyst estimates.

In July, Meta said it expected to spend $145 billion this year, nearly double what it spent in 2026.

Last week, Amazon said it expects to spend $220 billion this year, and Microsoft said it expected to spend $170 billion by the end of the year.

Alphabet’s latest forecast for spending is between $195 billion to $205 billion in 2026.

The iPhone-maker is in a legal battle with one of its close AI partners, though.

In July, Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly orchestrating a campaign to steal the iPhone maker’s trade secrets as the AI lab tries to develop its own consumer hardware device.

OpenAI’s flagship product, ChatGPT, has been integrated into Apple products since 2024.

items.title: Canada presenting itself as climate leader at COP31, despite policy rollbacks
items.description: Despite its rollbacks of climate policy, the Carney government will lead a delegation to the COP31 conference in Turkey next week presenting itself as an international climate leader.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Minister of Environment Julie Dabrusin rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Despite its rollbacks of climate policy, the Carney government will lead a delegation to the COP31 conference in Turkey next week presenting itself as an international climate leader.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada will present itself as an international climate leader when it sends a delegation to the annual UN climate talks next week in Turkey, despite its rollbacks of climate policy under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Government officials held a technical briefing for journalists Monday ahead of the annual two-week COP31 conference, the main forum for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the 2015 Paris climate pact.

That pact committed signatories to reducing emissions sharply to keep global warming below 2 C and as close as possible to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels by the end of this century. A UN report last month said that goal is now out of reach because emissions have not come down fast enough.

That report will be a key feature of the upcoming COP31, where discussions will address how to reduce emissions to keep warming below 2 C by 2100.

Government officials told the briefing on Monday that Canada remains a “credible international actor on climate change” that other countries are keen to engage with.

But Patrick Bonin, the Bloc Québécois environment critic who will attend COP31 as part of the Canadian delegation, said Canada’s track record of rolling back climate policy has harmed its international reputation.

“I can’t see how they can pivot over a few days during COP to have any credibility on climate change,” Bonin told The Canadian Press in French.

“We’re no longer in an era where Canada can lend itself to any credibility with its action plan on climate, since Canada is in the middle of completely halting its short-term goals and can’t meet its 2030 emission reduction goals until at least 2050.”

The government’s own numbers show Canada is nowhere close to meeting its international commitment to reduce emissions by at least 40 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030.

Since taking office Carney has rolled back a number of climate policies initiated by the former government under Justin Trudeau, including eliminating the consumer carbon price, adjusting standards for the industrial carbon price, repealing a mandate for electric vehicle sales, and cancelling a planned emissions cap on oil and gas production.

In a video released in June, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

That same month a number of Canada’s most prominent environmental groups, including the David Suzuki Foundation, Ecojustice, Greenpeace Canada, Nature Canada and Environmental Defence, pushed for meetings with Carney’s aides and MPs to discuss what they called “urgent concerns about the government’s moves to eviscerate environmental laws and procedures and to undermine Canada’s nature, climate and clean energy goals.”

Canada won the “fossil of the day” title at last year’s COP30 in Brazil. Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”

Carney will not attend the leaders’ summit at the start of the summit but Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin will be in Turkey for the first week of talks. Officials said she will convene a ministerial meeting with the European Union of the Global Methane Pledge, a group of 159 countries committed to collectively reducing global methane emissions by 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.

In June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched a global call to action on methane during an address at the London Climate Action Week.

Canadian officials on Monday said Canada will be “promoting” methane mitigation at COP31 as a “high-impact, cost-effective” way to address emissions.

In its latest annual national emissions report last month, the Canadian Climate Institute credited “fugitive methane emission reductions” as the main driver behind a lower level of emissions from Canada’s oil and gas sector in 2025, despite boosts in production.

But even on methane things have been slowed down as Canada delayed the implementation of its methane regulations.

Canada is also in the spotlight after the environment commissioner last week issued a report which found in 2024 the government abandoned work on a 2021 pledge to ban the export of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Government officials have since said the work is only “paused,” though the report said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Canada and the United Kingdom are the co-leaders of the Powering Past Coal alliance, which seeks to accelerate the transition off coal power around the world.

Government officials refused to say during Monday’s technical briefing whether Canada informed any of its international partners that its work to ban thermal coal exports had ended or was paused.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

items.title: New U.S. rules on flight delays may affect Canadian travellers. Here’s how
items.description: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Travellers stand in line as some flights are delayed at Houston Hobby Airport on March 16, 2026. (Ashley Landis / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Ashley Landis</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.
items.body:
New U.S. government rules on flight disruptions coming into force early next year could affect passengers coming from Canada, though experts are divided on whether they will have a significant impact.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), which published the new rules on the Federal Register daily journal in September, is reclassifying 10 types of events that cause flight delays and cancellations as outside the airline’s control. These events include a passenger’s death, unscheduled mechanical issues, severe weather, cybersecurity attacks and potential tech outages.

The rule was supposed to take effect Oct. 19 but was postponed until Feb. 1, 2027.

The department acknowledged in the notice that “the total value of amenities and compensation currently provided by air carriers to consumers will be reduced under this final rule.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said the new rules may mean travellers won’t be entitled to the same type of protections they used to have.

“So basically, it’s taking some of what was the responsibility of the airlines and recategorizing them … outside of the airline’s control,” Katy Nastro, a travel industry expert based in New York, said in a video interview with CTVNews.ca on Friday. “And very simply, for travellers, that means you may not be entitled to the same type of protections that you are now.”

“Now, when this new rule goes into effect, you as a passenger, if you are impacted due to an unscheduled maintenance event, this is outside of the airline’s control, meaning that they’re not now forced, or really obliged, to provide a hotel voucher or a meal voucher,” she added.

Airline passenger advocacy group FlyersRights is suing the U.S. Department of Transportation over the rules, which they say shift the costs from airline delays to passengers.

“A change in reporting classifications is not permission to reduce passenger rights,” Paul Hudson, president of FlyersRights, said in a news release Friday. “... The rule sneakily transfers costs from airlines back to passengers for delays involving mechanical problems that are the responsibility and fault of the airlines.”

Nastro, a correspondent with the Flighty flight-tracker app, said the change will affect anyone “travelling within the U.S., to the U.S., or from the U.S.,” regardless of their nationality or the airline, if their flight experiences certain types of disruptions that are now outside the airline’s control.

“In certain circumstances, it does grey the disruption category for consumers,” Nastro said. “This new regulation … just makes it even more confusing for travellers when they’re trying to navigate what exactly they’re entitled to in terms of disruption protections.”

Under the current DOT regulations, Nastro said disrupted flights may allow travellers to get hotel or meal vouchers, rebook flights or get refunds.

Gábor Lukács, president of Air Passenger Rights, said he believes the new rules would have no impact on Canadian travellers flying to or from Canada from the U.S. or via the U.S. because they would have some rights under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR). He said the APPR would also apply to those with U.S. connections on one ticket, such as a passenger who travels from Toronto to Beijing with a connection in San Francisco.

“People who actually just fly between Canada and the U.S. or fly to or from Canada via the U.S. will be unaffected at all,” Lukács said in a phone interview with CTVNews.ca.

However, he said Canadians who are not flying to Canada or from Canada are among those who will be affected by the new rules. This includes those who first drive over to the U.S., and then fly out from the U.S.

“The only time you would not be covered (is) if your travel has nothing to do with Canada,” he added. “… Just because you hold a Canadian passport, doesn’t mean that you can rely on the APPR. But if you started or ended your travel in Canada, then the APPR will apply to you.”

Still, he said Canada’s passenger protection regulations are “weak” with rules that are “unnecessarily complex” and “very difficult to enforce.”

He said the U.S. rule change’s effect is “primarily administrative,” because it involves how flight disruptions are being reported and passengers aren’t compensated in cash for flight disruptions in the U.S.

Lukács said the main issue with the new rules will be unexpected maintenance issues, which he said is “completely unreasonable.”

items.body:
CALGARY — The number of homes that changed hands in Calgary last month dropped 15.3 per cent compared with October 2025 as prices ticked lower overall.

The Calgary Real Estate Board says there were 1,592 home sales in October, as the residential benchmark price fell 0.4 per cent to $564,200.

The board’s chief economist Ann-Marie Lurie says much of the pressure on pricing is concentrated in higher-density housing types due to oversupply, while detached and semi-detached prices have remained more stable.

  • Most recent real estate news from BNNBloomberg.ca

Apartment-style homes saw a year-over-year price decline of 7.9 per cent to $288,800, and row-style properties were 5.1 per cent less expensive at $407,500 last month.

Detached home prices dipped 0.7 per cent to $735,100, while semi-detached prices moved 0.8 per cent higher compared with October 2025 to $685,200.

There were 2,928 new listings on the market in October, down 9.4 per cent from a year earlier, while total inventory was 4.6 per cent lower year-over-year to 6,173 homes for sale.

items.title: More drops for AI and tech stocks overshadow gains for most of Wall Street
items.description: A morning rally for U.S. stocks petered out as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Drew Cohen works on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Wednesday, April 2, 2025. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A morning rally for U.S. stocks petered out as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A morning rally for U.S. stocks petered out on Monday as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.

The S&P 500 sank 0.5 per cent after erasing a gain that had reached 1.1 per cent early in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213 points, or 0.4 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite fell 1.1 per cent.

The mixed performance for indexes came even though the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 climbed. They benefited from a 7.6 per cent drop for the price of a barrel of Brent crude to US$104.77. It’s the latest yo-yo move for oil prices on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly US$70 and US$120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began, and it’s been quick to reverse direction.

So have stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry, which have been shaky for months amid criticism that they surged too high and are in a bubble. Worries are growing that all the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centers won’t yield enough productivity and profit to make the investments worth it.

The latest profit reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also showed how AI may be dragging on their own businesses. Not only did Google’s parent company burn through more cash during the latest quarter, as measured by something called free cash flow, it also reported slower-than-expected growth in its search business, which raised worries about AI undercutting its cash cow. That caused Alphabet’s stock to drop more than 12 per cent Thursday for its worst day on record.

On Monday, Alphabet initially rallied 2.6 per cent, but it later erased the gain and then finished with a loss of 0.3 per cent. Nvidia, meanwhile, went from an early gain of 2.6 per cent to a drop of 1.3 per cent following its 4.2 per cent slide on Friday. Such swings dragged the rest of the market with them.

Adding to the weakness in tech was Marvell Technology, which fell 12.7 per cent after saying it would buy Lumentum. Marvell said it will give 4.5 of its shares for each share of Lumentum, which sells lasers and other products that power the networks and infrastructure behind AI and cloud computing. Lumentum’s shares fell 18.6 per cent.

Outside of AI and tech, the U.S. market did much better, and nearly seven out of every 10 stocks in the S&P 500 index rose.

Monday’s ease in oil prices helped lift stocks of companies with big fuel bills. United Airlines flew 4.8 per cent higher, Southwest Airlines climbed 3.6 per cent and cruise operator Carnival rose 4.2 per cent.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

Marriott International rose 4.3 per cent after reporting strength for its hotels around the world. Even in the Middle East, where the war has affected its business, CEO Anthony Capuano said that “trends improved meaningfully” from the spring.

Idexx Laboratories leaped 21.8 per cent after it likewise reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company, which sells diagnostic equipment and other products to veterinarians, also raised its forecasts for revenue and profit for the full year of 2026.

All told, the S&P 500 slipped 38.67 points to 7,541.40. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213.67 to 51,983.98, and the Nasdaq composite fell 272.68 to 25,164.32.

Expectations are high for all kinds of companies to continue to deliver big gains in profits as the U.S. economy keeps chugging along, even with high inflation and interest rates. That’s what helped send the S&P 500 to its record last month.

  • Latest updates on investing here

A report on Monday said that growth for U.S. manufacturing was better last month than economists expected. Perhaps just as importantly, a measure of inflation in the survey by the Institute for Supply Management showed prices were rising at a slower pace.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe.

The swings were larger in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2.2 per cent on renewed strength for the tech giants that dominate its market.

In China, indexes rose 1.1 per cent in Shanghai and 0.4 per cent in Hong Kong to recover some of their steep recent losses. Stocks in Shanghai finished October more than 15 per cent below a peak reached in May.

The People’s Bank of China said Monday that around 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) would be deployed under a new program that could help support the market.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

items.title: First Nation takes Ottawa to court over B.C. pipeline, alleging failure to consult
items.description: A Vancouver Island First Nation is taking the federal government to court, alleging Ottawa failed to properly consult its members before declaring a proposed oil pipeline a project of national interest.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Map showing the proposed Pacific Link pipeline corridors, which would carry crude oil from Bruderheim, Alta., to a planned export terminal near Delta, B.C. The final route has not yet been determined. (Pacific Link)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A Vancouver Island First Nation is taking the federal government to court, alleging Ottawa failed to properly consult its members before declaring a proposed oil pipeline a project of national interest.
items.body:
A Vancouver Island First Nation is taking the federal government to court, alleging Ottawa failed to properly consult its members before declaring a proposed oil pipeline a project of national interest.

W̱JOȽEȽP (Tsartlip First Nation) filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Oct. 30, challenging the designation of the proposed Pacific Link pipeline under the Building Canada Act.

The application alleges the government rushed the consultation process, provided insufficient information about the project and failed to adequately consider its potential impacts on the First Nation’s treaty rights.

At the heart of the challenge are Tsartlip’s rights under the 1852 North Saanich Treaty, which protects its members traditional fishing rights.

The First Nation says the proposed pipeline’s marine shipping route would pass through traditional fishing waters and harvesting areas around the Fraser River Delta and Strait of Georgia.

According to the court filing, federal officials consulted with Tsartlip between July 2 and Sept. 18, 2026. During that time, the First Nation says it repeatedly requested more information but received only general details about the project.

It also alleges Ottawa provided insufficient funding and imposed timelines that did not account for the community’s capacity to participate, including cultural and fishing activities during the summer.

Tsartlip submitted its concerns on Sept. 18, warning that consultation had not been adequate. Less than two weeks later, on Oct. 1, the federal government designated the pipeline a project of national interest.

Chief Curtis Olsen (TELX̱ILEM) says the decision puts the First Nation’s responsibilities to protect its traditional waters and future generations at risk.

“In 1852, the Crown made a promise in the Douglas Treaty that our people could continue to live from these waters as we always have,” Olsen said in a media release.

The designation has significant implications for how the project moves forward.

Under the Building Canada Act, certain federal authorizations are deemed to have been made in favour of the project once it receives national interest status. The legislation also allows exemptions from requirements under several federal laws, including the Fisheries Act and Impact Assessment Act.

Tsartlip argues that effectively moves key regulatory decisions ahead before the project has been fully developed or its impacts properly assessed.

The First Nation is also asking the court to rule that Ottawa must consult with it and obtain its consent before making another decision about the pipeline’s national interest designation.

The legal challenge also invokes the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Canada’s legislation implementing it.

“The consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months. That’s not efficient, that’s reckless,” said Adam Olsen (SȾHENEP), Tsartlip’s director of intergovernmental relations in a release.

The proposed Pacific Link pipeline would transport approximately one million barrels of crude oil per day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a new export terminal and offshore loading facility near Delta, B.C. The proposed route would stretch approximately 1,200 to 1,250 kilometres.

The court challenge could have implications beyond this project. Roberts Bank Terminal 2 has also been listed for consideration under the Building Canada Act, while Bill C-39, currently before Parliament, would make the national interest designation process permanent and allow entire regions to be designated.

Cold Lake First Nation has also filed its own application for judicial review challenging the Pacific Link designation.

Tsartlip says the pipeline could still move forward through the usual regulatory process. Its challenge is focused on whether the federal government followed its legal obligations before making the national interest designation.

CTV News has reached out to Pacific Link, Trans Mountain Corporation, Pembina Pipeline Corporation and the office of federal Minister Dominic LeBlanc for interviews and comment on the legal challenge. This story will be updated as responses are received.

The Federal Court has not yet ruled on the application.

items.description:

The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses […]

The post Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian banks see more losses from delinquent mortgages in their future—a lot more losses. Mortgage loss expectations have 3x since 2019.
items.body:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses has more than doubled over the past four years.

Canadian Banks Expect Mortgage Losses To Climb Sharply

Ratio of expected credit losses to total residential mortgage balances.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Lenders need to be prepared for losses on bad loans. It doesn’t matter how much borrowers are vetted; the reality is some won’t be fully repaid. To account for this, lenders record an allowance for credit losses—an estimate of the money they do not expect to recover. It reflects expected losses, not just losses that have already occurred. Those expectations have risen sharply.

The CMHC compared each bank’s mortgage portfolio against its allowance for credit losses. The median—half of banks are better, half are worse—had an allowance equivalent to $149 per $100,000 in mortgages in Q2 2026, up 13.2% from a year earlier. That share has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, more than doubling. It has roughly tripled (+202.8%) since Q2 2019, back in the before times.

Keep in mind that these measure expected losses relative to mortgage balances. The banks are preparing for higher losses on each dollar lent, and they’ve lent a lot more dollars over that period. Their expectations of losses have grown alongside their mortgage portfolio over the past 7 years.

Canadian Mortgage Losses Expected To Rise Further At Some Banks

The median bank’s increase is sharp, but it hides a much sharper climb at some banks. The 75th percentile, the threshold for the top 25% of banks, saw allowances reach $337 per $100,000 in mortgages, up 47.9% from last year. The share is more than double (+126%) the median, and the highest in the data going back to 2015.

Canadian Mortgage Loss Expectations Grew At 3 In 4 Banks

Most banks expect higher mortgage losses, with roughly 3 in 4 reporting higher allowances than a year earlier. That share was just 53% a year prior, an already tenfold increase from the 5% recorded in Q2 2022. The share of banks reporting higher expected losses has gone from only 1 in 20 banks to 3 in 4 over just four years.

While the amount remains small relative to total mortgage debt, the increase is hard to ignore. Banks are preparing to lose more of each dollar lent, and more lenders expect losses to grow. That also only captures part of the rising pressure, with distress rising even faster among mortgage investment entities (MIEs).

items.title: As hopes of a Canada-US deal rise, here’s what’s at stake for housing
items.description: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.content: <p>Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639292419264737498.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.body:
Formal talks between Canada and the US on a resolution to the tariff war could begin soon after prime minister Mark Carney’s Sunday social media post describing a productive recent discussion on the issue with US president Donald Trump.

Trade tensions have weighed against Canada’s economic outlook since the beginning of last year and emerged as a significant factor in the housing market’s continued malaise, pushing plenty of potential homebuyers to the sidelines and damaging consumer confidence.

While discussions between US and Canadian negotiators have yet to resume, a positive resolution to the trade war could have big implications for the national housing market.

Prospects for a 2027 recovery, some mortgage professionals say, could hinge massively on whether tariff tensions ease.

And Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) has highlighted how the trade war is worsening the mortgage strain for many borrowers in tariff-impacted parts of the country such as Southern Ontario, which has borne the brunt of US levies on steel, aluminum, automotive vehicles and parts, and agricultural products.

With homebuilding also taking a hit, the national housing agency’s deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional a swift end to the trade war could potentially improve the currently dire construction outlook.

“I’m a little bit concerned on the housing supply situation that higher interest rates are affecting developers,” he said. “Now on that side, if the situation were resolved, then maybe developers would have a lot more confidence in home construction.

“From a long-term affordability [perspective], that would be positive. I think if the overall uncertainty lowered… it would give renewed confidence to people who want to go out and buy a home. If you knew the dispute was over, I think that greater certainty would help the overall economy.”

Leaders’ comments suggest potential relief for borrowers ahead

Last week, Trump told a rally in Michigan that the trade war could be settled “pretty soon,” as he stepped up campaigning ahead of the crucial midterm elections, set to take place on November 3.

Trump and Carney’s recent statements mark the first hint of a possible détente since an end to tariff negotiations in August triggered a sudden escalation in the trade war.   

Ab Iorwerth said the ongoing trade war is part of the reason mortgage strain seems worse in Southern Ontario than other parts of the country, even though there’s no sign of a wider mortgage meltdown caused by rising arrears.

“There’s a lot of protection within the system so I don’t think we’re looking at a systemic issue, but there’s a lot of people being adversely impacted by what’s happening to them individually,” he said. “And I think a lot of households are facing challenges with these higher interest rates that they’re bearing and the uncertainty over the trajectory of mortgage rates.

“There’s still that lingering concern over inflation and then there’s uncertainty on the macroeconomic front with trade. So I think all of this is creating a lot of stress for individual households about what might happen.”

Iran and inflation add further complications for housing

While tariffs were the defining story of 2025 for the Canadian economy, they’ve been joined this year by surging fuel prices because of the war in Iran – another curveball that could complicate the picture even if the trade war ends.

Those higher fuel prices have sparked fears of a wider spillover into headline inflation, one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada opted to hike its benchmark interest rate last week for the first time in over three years.

Against that backdrop, the central bank doesn’t see the housing market bouncing back in 2027 – although it underlined the positive effects an end to the trade war could potentially have.

A Canada-US deal reducing tariffs “would increase exports and business investment, boosting employment and incomes,” the BoC said in its latest Monetary Policy Report. “Higher demand could increase the pass-through from higher energy prices. The removal of counter-tariffs would provide an offset.”

items.description: Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower
items.content: <p>Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639292444699523088.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower
items.body:
The alternative lending space is changing – and as the big banks continue tightening their lending criteria, alt lenders are seeing their market share grow. At MortgageFest, we caught up with Haventree Bank chief operating officer Joe Cote to hear his thoughts on current trends and what’s in store for the sector down the line.

[00:00] There's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s, but we're talking about life happens. Brokers are small business owners. This affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years and the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers.

[00:30] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So, next up we have Joe Cote, Chief Operating Officer at HipBilt Bank, whose booth we see just over here. Have you been having many productive conversations with brokers today?

[00:40] Joe Cote: Lots of discussions. I certainly think that there's been a lot of changes throughout the industry, specifically with HipBilt, which is very exciting. And having a lot of brokers come back and are interested to see, you know, tell me more. Tell me what you're doing. We're hearing a lot of exciting things that have been happening over the course of the last 6 to 12 months. Tell me what's happening over the course of the next 6 to 12 months and how can we partner together?

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And the event is happening at a really interesting time for the industry. I mean, not that we haven't had any non-eventful times over the past few years. It's just been one thing after the next. But 2026, how are you assessing the market this year? How's it been?

[01:13] Joe Cote: I think obviously the market has had a fairly large impact on a lot of brokers and a lot of lenders, the community at large. We are still very happy and fortunate with our position and our performance so far this year. We've got great partners. I think that value proposition that we have certainly been working on has been what, the proof in the pudding of being able to look to those partners. We've got a lot of partners that have come back. I think that they're very excited with the service, the products, and the relationships that we've built. And from an overall performance standpoint, we're going to finish the year actually fairly strong and we got some good growth prospects for 2027.

[01:45] Fergal McAlinden: I was interested to hear, Joe, from lenders about borrower types. We know that they've evolved a lot over the past few years. I'm wondering if there's a specific type of borrower that you feel best placed to cater to in the current market.

[01:57] Joe Cote: I think the short answer to that is there's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. Well, I think one of the opportunities has certainly been around the evolution of the alt space and how it's very much part of the prime offering now. And it used to be around bruised credit, which is still very much the case and will always be part of the ideal client profile that the alt space was built off of.

[02:18] But now we look at the tightening credit box from a lot of the larger Schedule 1 banks. That business flow, as it's been tightening, has actually been coming into the alternative space. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s. But we're talking about life happens. We're talking about divorces. We're talking about CRA. Multiple properties, business for self.

[02:43] It doesn't necessarily mean bruised credit anymore. It just means maybe not as simple from a credit profile standpoint. So, we are truly running the entire gamut of what I would say is the alternative space is now alt A through to what was bruised credit before. And I'd love to see the evolution of the space and the value that we're bringing back to the Canadian consumers.

[03:04] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And I think that evolution, nobody's expecting that to slow anytime soon, especially with how the market is this year and some of the challenges being faced by buyers. When it comes to brokers, how have you been dealing with them this year? Are there any kind of approaches you've been keeping in mind with brokers?

[03:19] Joe Cote: Yeah, a big emphasis of our partnership model with brokers has been, how do we just focus on building our processes, our expectations, our interaction models completely around the broker community. And thinking about brokers as small business owners.

[03:34] I've been saying this a lot just recently on stage. I think the biggest thing was around brokers are small business owners. It is all about the experience. It's about the referral business. And if they land a great client experience based on the partnership that they have with the lender, that client's going to come back. They're going to refer more business.

[03:52] And that alternative space, again, especially in the small business community and or gig economy, we've got so many borrowers that are looking for solutions that they didn't even know existed before. So, we've basically repositioned, I would say, a lot of our processes and policies to be built around brokers and the client experience, keeping that really at heart.

[04:10] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Looking ahead, 2027, hard as it is to believe, is just around the corner. Any trends that you're keeping an eye on or anything that you're expecting to be a big factor next year?

[04:20] Joe Cote: It's too fast. I miss summer already. I would say the trend, if anything, is probably going to be continuing. If you think about it, a couple of things. One has been the compounding effect of the interest rate environment, the tariffs, both in terms of just cost of goods as well as taxation on it, especially for small business owners.

[04:40] All those financing needs actually aren't going away. The financing needs are going to increase, especially if you think about this affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years. That's taxing a lot of Canadians, and that problem's not going to get any easier in the current environment.

[04:56] Not only what's happening with Canada and the US, but certainly I think in terms of the interest rate environment over the course of the next 12 months, there's not a single person that's expecting interest rates to stay flat. In that increasing environment, it's going to only compound the problem, and brokers are going to need to understand that business model.

[05:15] They're going to need to find ways to actually support their clients who are going to have needs, and knowing full well that the traditional means of prime sourcing is not necessarily going to be as viable as it used to be historically. And the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers that are not currently accessing the alt space like they should be.

[05:27] Fergal McAlinden: For sure, and on that rate question, as you mentioned, I think we're all just strapped in waiting to see what happens on the bond market and on trade war and everything.

[05:34] Joe Cote: Yeah.

[05:34] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah, the only thing that's certain is that we have more uncertainty ahead, I think, is the way to put it. Maybe just one last word on the event, Joe. Have you met your target audience, and we'll be seeing you next year?

[05:43] Joe Cote: Absolutely. It's been wonderful, actually. Not only have I met, from an audience perspective, everybody in terms of our partners, as well as potential net new partners, both in terms of brokers, as well as a lot of other broker ancillary partners here.

[05:58] I think about the technology providers, I think about net new products that are coming on the market. I can point to a couple over there, which I just think are phenomenal in terms of the innovation that is showcased at the event, and I love being part of it, hearing the stories, how we can better service our clients.

[06:12] And looking at these partner solutions on how we can kind of improve the experience, I will definitely be back.

[06:15] Fergal McAlinden: Love to hear it. Okay, great stuff. Thank you for stopping by. Much appreciated. Then enjoy the rest of the event.

[06:19] Joe Cote: Thanks for having me.

Ontario credit unions grew assets and posted sharply stronger year-over-year profits in the second quarter of 2026, even as deeper loan arrears kept building, according to the latest Sector Outlook Report from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA).

Sector assets across the 48 institutions reached $106.47 billion at June 30, up 4.24% year over year.

Return on average assets (ROAA), the regulator’s core profitability measure, rose to 46 basis points from 30, as deposit costs fell faster than loan income.

One basis point equals 0.01%.

Credit union mortgage delinquency eases, but deeper arrears build

Residential mortgages remain the sector’s anchor. Credit unions held $57.92 billion in home loans at quarter-end, up 2.68% year over year, while commercial lending rose 1.97% to $27.44 billion.

The share of residential mortgages more than 30 days past due slipped to 1.13% from 1.15% in the first quarter, helping total 30-day delinquency record its first quarterly decline since the third quarter of 2024.

Year over year, though, mortgage delinquency was up 21 basis points, and commercial delinquency jumped 98 basis points to 2.80%.

The report’s tables point to strain further down the pipeline.

Loans more than 90 days delinquent rose to 1.08% of the total book from 0.99% in the first quarter and 0.71% a year earlier, while loan-loss allowances jumped 37.2% to $399 million.

Five of the 48 credit unions posted negative returns.

That mirrors the wider province, where Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) expects Ontario mortgage arrears to keep worsening until mid-2027.

CMHC deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth flagged the regional split in an October interview on trade-driven rate volatility and arrears.

“We’re watching arrears and delinquencies very closely. They’re particularly acute in Toronto, less so in Vancouver,” ab Iorwerth said.

“It’s just that they’re going up quite rapidly and it’s a source of concern. Maybe I should extend it beyond Toronto to include southern Ontario as well – but then you have places like Alberta where the economy remains strong and arrears and delinquencies remain contained.”

Jessica Rickerby, President of CMBA-ON, and Aled ab Iorwerth, Deputy Chief Economist at CMHC, warn that rising interest rates could further challenge housing affordability and prolong mortgage renewal pressures for Canadian borrowers. https://t.co/9P0c7D7qBi — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 2, 2026

What does the FSRA outlook mean for broker files?

The quarter predates tighter policy: the Bank of Canada held at 2.25% through June, then raised its rate to 2.50% on October 28.

Credit unions enter that shift with liquidity up 45 basis points to 12.88% and borrowings down 25.25%.

Lenders in the broker channel are already sharpening scrutiny. Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, spoke on a MortgageFest Canada panel on prime lending in September.

“We are very focused on making sure that the story and the documentation and the numbers align,” she said.

“Having those conversations upfront and telling that clear and concise story is going to allow underwriters to make a decision faster.”

FSRA said it issued the first edition of its Enhanced Data Collection Supplemental Report in September, with the next edition expected in the first quarter of 2027.

items.title: FSRA bars Ontario mortgage agent after Tribunal finds dishonesty
items.description: Alongside the licence refusal, FSRA imposed $15,000 in administrative penalties
items.content: <p>Alongside the licence refusal, FSRA imposed $15,000 in administrative penalties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639292393193875248.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Alongside the licence refusal, FSRA imposed $15,000 in administrative penalties
items.body:
Ontario’s mortgage industry watchdog has barred a former mortgage agent from the province’s broker market after a regulatory tribunal found him responsible for three separate contraventions, including allowing himself to be used to facilitate dishonesty.

The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has refused to renew the licence of Raouf Ghadrdoust, who held a Level 1 mortgage agent licence from July 1, 2008, until March 31, 2023.

Alongside the licence refusal, FSRA imposed $15,000 in administrative penalties, following an order signed on October 14, by Troy Harrison, Acting Director of Litigation and Enforcement, by delegated authority from FSRA’s chief executive officer.

The Financial Services Tribunal held an electronic hearing across three days in June, concluding that Ghadrdoust had contravened the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 (MBLAA).

Its Reasons for Decision, dated October 1, directed FSRA’s chief executive to implement the proposed penalties and licence refusal in full.

Three violations behind the decision

The Tribunal identified three distinct contraventions. Ghadrdoust was found to have dealt in mortgages for remuneration outside his licensed brokerage, in breach of section 2(3) of the MBLAA.

He also received remuneration from a person other than his registered brokerage, contrary to section 4(1) of Ontario Regulation 187/08.

The third and most serious finding was that he allowed himself to be used to facilitate dishonesty, in violation of section 3.1 of the same regulation.

Ghadrdoust applied to renew his licence on March 24, 2023. A Notice of Proposal to refuse that renewal was issued on September 3, 2024, with the resulting Tribunal hearing upholding the regulator’s position in its entirety.

Under the October order, Ghadrdoust must pay the $15,000 penalty within 30 days, or the debt becomes enforceable as an order of the Superior Court of Justice.

Brokers weigh in on rising enforcement standards

The case arrives as FSRA has sharply escalated its enforcement posture across Ontario’s mortgage sector.

The regulator’s first-ever annual enforcement report, released earlier this year amid a broader surge in mortgage industry penalties, revealed that mortgage-related sanctions in 2025 totalled approximately $860,000 – a roughly 50% increase over the prior year.

Two of the three contraventions – dealing outside a licensed brokerage and accepting fees from a non-registered party – mirror the provisions at the centre of FSRA’s February action against former agent Shan Jamal.

He received $20,000 in penalties for arranging multiple off-book mortgage deals and routing payments through other entities to avoid detection.

The “facilitating dishonesty” finding under section 3.1 of Ontario Regulation 187/08 has also appeared in a significantly larger case: FSRA fined former agent Lin Liang $275,000 after she brokered 15 deals connected to an alleged fraud scheme, with the Tribunal finding she ought to have known she was being used to facilitate dishonesty, the same standard applied against Ghadrdoust.

For many established brokers, the trajectory is long overdue. Joe Sammut, broker of record at Mortgage Architects – A Better Way in Ontario, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the crackdown marked a meaningful shift in how the regulator views the profession.

“I’ve seen more cases against bad actors in the last 12 to 18 months than in previous years,” Sammut said.

“They seem to be clamping down and cleaning up, and they’re making sure the fines they’re enacting on people are publicized.”

Carmen Costa, principal broker and owner at TCG Lending Centres in Ontario, echoed the view that tougher oversight ultimately serves the industry’s best interests.

“Mortgage brokers deal with complex products that can have long-term financial consequences for consumers, so strong oversight is important,” she told CMP in an interview on Ontario’s regulatory landscape.

items.content: <p>OREA praised Ontario’s housing measures – but one extension could determine who truly benefits</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639292266160812841.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: OREA praised Ontario’s housing measures – but one extension could determine who truly benefits
items.body:
The Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) has welcomed Ontario’s 2026 Fall Economic Statement, tabled by Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy on October 29. But the association is pressing the Ford government to extend its new-home harmonised sales tax (HST) relief beyond March 2027, warning the current deadline limits how many buyers can benefit.

Acting Chief Executive Officer Diane J. Brisebois, speaking for OREA’s nearly 100,000 REALTOR Members across the province, credited the Ford government for advancing both the $8.8-billion Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build and temporary HST relief on new homes valued up to $1 million, two measures OREA has long advocated for.

“These types of bold actions, including their promise to continue funding and supporting municipalities that already do not levy development charges, will have a positive effect within many parts of our economy,” Brisebois said.

“It will help expand critical infrastructure, enable more housing supply to hit the market, lower the cost of homes, and create good-paying jobs.”

What Ontario’s 2026 fall economic statement delivered

Tabled against a projected $16.9-billion deficit, up from $13.8 billion in the March 2026 budget, the statement reaffirmed several key housing and economic measures.

Chief among them for the mortgage industry: the 10-year, $8.8-billion Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build, designed to fund housing-enabling infrastructure and reduce municipal development charges, and temporary HST relief on new homes valued up to $1 million, providing up to $130,000 in savings per eligible transaction.

The statement also confirmed an $8.7-billion Canada-Ontario action plan to shield Ontario’s industrial base from ongoing US tariff pressures.

Statistics Canada reported no growth in August GDP and an estimated decline in September, suggesting third-quarter growth may fall short of the Bank of Canada’s expectations following its latest interest rate increase. https://t.co/CCruoYeDlc — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 30, 2026

Development charges: OREA’s core demand

Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) data on how soaring development charges are reshaping Canada’s housing costs shows per-unit levies for a two-bedroom apartment ranging from approximately $39,600 in Ottawa to $121,500 in Markham, representing between 8% and 16% of new condo prices in parts of Ontario.

Kim Fairley, president of OREA, previously said the package delivers meaningful relief even for buyers well beyond Toronto.

“We’re talking homes up to $130,000 in a price difference,” Fairley said.

“That’s a big deal. Even for me up in Sault Ste. Marie — our new homes average between $600,000 and $700,000. Even for that spectrum, that’s a big difference for people up in the northern areas to have that swing into their favour when it comes to being able to buy that house.”

Brokers weigh in on ground-level impact

Despite OREA’s positive reception, concerns remain that development charge reform may fall short without coordinated municipal follow-through.

Matthew O’Neil of Connolly Capital in Toronto was candid about the pricing gap that continues to face first-time condo buyers.

“The problem with pre-con pricing is that even after this new rebate, it’s still priced way higher than resale,” O’Neil previously told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“If you’re a first-time buyer and you want to buy a condo downtown, why would you buy preconstruction? It makes no sense. You’re looking at $1,300, $1,400, $1,500 a square foot — but you can go buy a resale condo for under $1,000 a square foot.”

OREA has specifically called for the HST rebate deadline to be pushed past March 31, 2027, to allow more families to access the measure.

Micky Khaneka of MKG Mortgages in Toronto told Canadian Mortgage Professional — amid ongoing questions around Ontario’s HST New Housing Rebate and how relief is applied at the point of sale — that the initiative still sends a clear market signal.

“I definitely think it’s a signal that the government’s listening and they’re really trying to reprioritize this because taking that out helps,” Khaneka said.

items.title: Christopher Liew: Warning signs your parents’ finances are off track
items.description: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew goes over the warning signs that your parents are struggling financially, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.
items._ogDesc: Personal finance contributor Christopher Liew goes over the warning signs that your parents are struggling financially, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.
items.body:
Christopher Liew is a CFP® professional and CFA charterholder. He shares insights on personal finance with thousands of Canadian readers at Blueprint Financial.

A lot of us grow up assuming our parents have money figured out. They paid the bills, worried about our tuition, and never asked us for a thing. So when that starts to change, it can sneak up on you.

In my experience, by the time a parent asks for help, the problem has been building for years. Below, I’ll walk through the warning signs that you may be about to become your parents’ financial safety net, and how to step in without wrecking your own retirement.

Why more families are feeling this now

The pressure on retirees is growing. In the National Institute on Ageing’s 2025 survey, only 29 per cent of Canadians 50 and older who haven’t retired yet said they could afford to retire when they wanted, down from 35 per cent in 2022.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The people stepping in are stretched too. As CTV News reported in May, more than half of Canada’s caregivers are juggling paid work alongside caring for a loved one, and many say the pressure is becoming too much.

That being said, money trouble doesn’t always look like a crisis. From what I’ve seen with clients, it shows up in small ways first.

1. They’re paying everyday bills with credit or the house

If your parents are carrying a credit card balance month to month, opening a line of credit, or tapping a home equity line of credit (HELOC) to cover groceries and property tax, pay attention. Borrowing for a new roof is one thing. Borrowing to keep the lights on means their income no longer covers their life.

Home equity is the one that worries me most. A reverse mortgage or HELOC can make sense as part of a real plan, but when it’s used to plug a monthly gap, the interest quietly eats the cushion they’ll need for care later.

You may never see their statements, but you’ll notice the clues: talk of consolidating debt, new cards showing up in the mail, or a sudden interest in refinancing a house they owned outright. If you’re seeing more than one of these, it’s worth a gentle question the next time you visit.

2. Their income is mostly CPP and OAS

In my view, CPP and OAS were never meant to fund a whole retirement on their own. If your parents don’t have a workplace pension or meaningful RRSP or RRIF savings, they may be living right at the edge.

One way to gauge it is the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which tops up low-income seniors. A single senior needs annual income (not counting OAS) under $23,112 to qualify, so a parent anywhere near that line has very little room for surprises. GIS is based on the previous year’s tax return, so make sure they’re still filing every spring.

I’d also watch for a parent who started CPP at 60 because they needed the cash, not as a strategy. Taking it early cuts the payment by up to 36 per cent, and that reduction is permanent.

3. They’ve started asking for help “just this once”

The first request might be small. A car repair, a dental bill, a month of rent. Saying yes is natural, and I’d never tell you not to help your parents, but one-off help has a way of turning into a monthly transfer.

Before you commit to anything regular, figure out what you can give without pausing your own RRSP or TFSA contributions. One of the biggest regrets I see in retirees is giving money to family before securing their own future, and I walked through that and nine other regrets in a recent Blueprint Financial video. The same logic applies when the money flows up to your parents instead of down to your kids.

And if you have kids, you could be squeezed from both directions. In a 2026 BMO survey, 49 per cent of Canadians said they plan to help their adult children financially, and 83 per cent of that group said they understand it will hurt their own retirement.

4. There’s no clear plan if their health changes

This is the sign that turns a manageable situation into an emergency. If you don’t know where their accounts are, whether they have a will, or who holds power of attorney, you’ll be scrambling at the worst possible time.

You don’t need every detail on Day 1. I’d start with a simple list of where their accounts are, copies of their will and power of attorney documents, and the name of anyone who already helps them with money, like an accountant or advisor.

I covered how to start that conversation in my CTV News column on talking to aging parents about money. If you’re also noticing confusion around bills or unusual withdrawals, I wrote about those red flags in my piece on money mistakes that can signal cognitive decline.

If your parent relies on you for basics like food and shelter because of a physical or mental infirmity, look into the federal Canada caregiver credit. They don’t have to live with you to qualify.

Final thoughts

Spotting these signs doesn’t mean your parents failed, and it doesn’t mean you’re on the hook forever. It means you still have time, which is the most valuable thing you can have here.

Have the honest conversation early, decide what you can realistically offer, and protect your own plan while you do it. Helping your parents shouldn’t turn you into the next generation that can’t afford to retire.

items.description: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.content: <p>Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639289754495839586.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank sees a sluggish outlook continuing – and BMO managing director says less focus on housing wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada doesn’t see much chance of a hotter national housing market in the near future, forecasting this week that housing will contribute essentially nothing to national economic growth in the next two years.

The central bank said in the latest Monetary Policy Report, released alongside its rate hike on Wednesday, that climbing borrowing costs will send housing-related expenses higher in 2027 and 2028, while material and equipment prices will also increase as home construction and maintenance costs rise.

That’s not to say housing and mortgage professionals will notice a sudden or sharp change, with the deep freeze that’s gripped the market over the past two years showing no sign of thawing.

Benjamin Reitzes (pictured top), managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist at Bank of Montreal (BMO), told Canadian Mortgage Professional the central bank’s 25-basis-point increase on October 28 may have a slight negative impact on the market, but that there wasn’t much momentum to stall in the first place.

“What’s notable is that you already had mortgage rates notably higher right across the curve. So the only point where they were contained was on the variable side,” he said. “At least half the activity was coming in variable, according to the data.

“So [the hike] will provide a bit more of a dampener, I think, on the margin. Of course it makes a difference – but it’s not as if housing was booming. And so there probably is a limit to how much weaker it gets.”

Why the housing market is still slow

The main culprits for the still-sluggish housing market are well known at this stage: economic uncertainty triggered by the US-Canada trade war, and inflation concerns as a result of surging fuel costs.

That trade dispute has sparked fears of job losses and a big hit to the economy since the beginning of last year, while rising inflation was one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada raised rates on Wednesday and could hike again soon.

And while home prices have slid across many markets in 2025 and 2026, Reitzes suggested that the correction may still have a while to run.

“The reality for the housing market is that affordability is still stretched. There’s still room for prices to fall – the affordability side of things needs to improve,” he said. “I think at this point, the path of least resistance is probably still toward modestly lower prices for housing and continued softness on that front. And that’s what the Bank’s expecting.”

Affordability improved in almost every major Canadian market in September, according to ratehub.ca, but that picture could be complicated if rates continue rising in the coming months.

Population dynamics are also playing their part in the market’s slowdown. The federal government dramatically upped its immigration targets in the early years of this decade, boosting demand for housing and rental units.

Those targets have been pared back substantially, a trend that’s lowered clamour for condo rentals in major markets – most notably Toronto – and contributed to the wider housing market cooldown.

The market’s torpor has also fuelled calls among some executives for an end or revision to the foreign homebuyer ban that’s been in place since the beginning of 2023, although industry views on the matter have been mixed.

Why a less intense housing market could ultimately benefit Canada

Reitzes emphasized that a less intense focus on the housing market could be a net positive in the long run for the Canadian economy.

“Population growth is not particularly strong in Canada at the moment, and so the dynamics are challenging for housing – and that isn’t necessarily the worst thing,” he said. “Housing has… gotten too much attention over the past few decades, and it’s kind of shifting the focus toward business investment and toward driving productivity growth in Canada.

“As much as people love to focus on housing, sometimes it’s not always the best use of capital for the country. So it’s not the end of the world here that we’re going a different way.”

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories include Canada’s real estate spreading beyond Ontario and BC, and the CMHC warns mortgage arrears are set to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian GDP Stalls, Propped Up By Retail And Credit Cards

Canadian economic output is starting to struggle. Real GDP was flat for a second straight month in August, with only 9 out of 20 industrial sectors showing growth. Stalling appears to be an optimistic take though, as the details are a little more ominous. The pillars supporting the data were higher retail sales (mostly food) and credit card use. In other words, grocery spending and credit card debt are keeping the economy afloat. That’s more concerning given the increasing use of credit cards to make ends meet, according to TransUnion.

Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse

The arrears rate at Canadian banks has made an aggressive climb and it’s not over, warns the CMHC. The CBA arrears rate has more than doubled from record lows over the past 5 years, hitting 0.29% in July—an 11-year high. The rate will climb through mid-2027, the end of the agency’s forecast period. They cite price corrections in BC and Ontario persisting as the key reason. However, prices are near record highs in other provinces and have only just begun to correct, suggesting risk is further to the upside.

Bank of Canada Sees Elevated Inflation Into 2028, Housing To Remain Weak

The Bank of Canada’s (BoC) got 99 problems and inflation’s just one—until 2028, at least that’s what they think. This week the BoC hiked its overnight rate to 2.5%, its first hike in over 3 years. Higher energy prices will trickle into broader consumer inflation, warns the BoC. As a result, headline CPI’s annual growth will remain above 3% into late 2027, returning to the 2% target by mid-2028. Just 2 more years to flatten the (inflation) curve?

Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces

Prices across the country surged when rates were cut in 2020. The national index has fallen 22.5% since prices peaked in 2022, when rates began to normalize. However, that correction was almost entirely the work of Ontario and—to a lesser extent—BC. The rest of the provinces remain near record highs, but that may be finally changing. Prices in some of those provinces have recently begun to make record-setting declines.

Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply

BoC researchers looked at the impact of monetary stimulus on housing supply. They found that rate cuts during a housing boom boost home building by 6%, but only 20% of that is due to financing. The remaining 80% of stimulus comes from the excess demand, as profits and prices rise too. They warn ignoring shelter costs during a housing boom can lead to an aggressive climb in prices. However, there’s an area of shelter inflation the BoC should ignore—mortgage interest. Mortgage interest’s inclusion in CPI creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Cutting rates reduces mortgage interest, signaling the need for more rate cuts. It’s a problem we’ve noted before, warning the circular logic is avoided by most countries.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC

Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate at banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, 52% higher than last year and 5x the low in 2022. That’s only the bank rate though, which makes the picture look better than reality. High-risk borrowers get booted to mortgage investment entities (MIEs), where risk is exploding. MIEs have seen the arrears rate around Greater Toronto surge from 3% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026, 3x the national MIE rate. They may only be a small share of national activity, but the bulk of their business is concentrated in one area—along with risk.

items.content: <p>The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_637746489857378440.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The CMAs are Canada's top mortgage industry night — and the ROI extends well beyond individual recognition
items.body:
For mortgage brokers and brokerage leaders across Canada, the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) have long represented the industry's highest standard of professional recognition.

Now in their 20th year, the CMAs are set to take place on November 25 at Rebel Toronto — and this milestone edition makes a compelling case for attending not as an individual, but as a team.

While individual nominations drive the night's agenda, the strategic value of group attendance at the CMAs extends far beyond the trophy.

For brokerages thinking seriously about recruitment, retention, culture, and competitive positioning, booking a table, or a block of seats, is increasingly less a luxury and more a sound business decision.

The case for a team night out

Mortgage brokerage is, at its core, a people business. The culture a firm builds internally — how it celebrates wins, how it acknowledges hard work, how it signals that individual effort is seen — has a direct effect on retention.

In an industry where top brokers face constant competition for their services, that culture gap can be costly.

Attending the CMAs as a group is one of the more tangible ways a brokerage can make that message concrete.

The event's November 25 evening at Rebel Toronto begins with a cocktail reception from 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony and dinner banquet until 10:30 p.m., with a post-awards celebration running well into the night.

It is not a brief industry function — it is a full evening designed, in the words of the organizers, for sharing insights, networking and building connections.

For a brokerage principal, bringing a group of agents or support staff signals something that a memo cannot: that their contributions are worth celebrating in public, before their peers, in the same room as hundreds of the foremost mortgage professionals and key executives from top Canadian organizations.

Secure a table at the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards and celebrate your team’s achievements alongside industry leaders, innovators, and top-performing professionals from across the country. #MortgageAwardsCA Book your table today: https://t.co/SSKx4yuft5 https://t.co/f31Lgyrrzt — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Recognition that reaches beyond the individual

The CMAs span 26 award categories, recognising brokers, brokerages, lenders, business development managers, underwriters, and service providers across the Canadian mortgage industry.

Across those categories, the awards are designed to reflect not just individual performance but the collective effort behind it.

When a broker wins, or is named an excellence awardee ahead of the November gala, the recognition lands in Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP) magazine and across its online channels.

The profiles and features generated from shortlistings and wins carry the names of those firms into editorial content that reaches CMP's readership throughout the year. For a brokerage, that coverage is institutional: it attaches to the firm's brand, not only to the individual.

That makes the case for corporate attendance straightforward. A team present in the room when a colleague is recognised associates the brokerage with the win in a way that a congratulatory email the next morning cannot replicate.

The CMAs have been described by past winners, including Steven Ranson of HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, as "iconic" — an event where the industry turns out to take stock of itself. Being part of that moment, collectively, carries a different weight than watching it from outside.

For brokerages that have not yet submitted a nomination, the deadline has passed for the 2026 cycle, with excellence awardees already announced in September.

But the event itself remains open to the industry, and registering as a group for the CMAs gala at Rebel Toronto is a separate matter from the nomination process.

The networking case for corporate attendance

Beyond recognition, the CMAs function as one of the most concentrated networking events on the Canadian mortgage calendar.

Hundreds of senior professionals — brokers, lenders, aggregators, and executives — gather in a single venue for an evening built around industry conversation.

The cocktail reception that opens the night is specifically designed to facilitate that kind of contact before the formal programme begins.

For a junior broker or an agent new to the industry, attending the CMAs alongside experienced colleagues offers a different kind of access.

The introductions that happen organically in rooms like Rebel Toronto — between a new agent and a business development manager from a major lender, or between a brokerage's team and a potential referral partner — are not easily manufactured in any other setting.

A group presence makes those introductions more natural: arriving as a team, rather than alone, lowers the social friction of a large industry event.

For mortgage professionals seeking deeper insight into how Canada's top brokerages and lenders benchmark their performance, events like the CMAs serve as a live read on where the industry's weight is shifting — which firms are growing, which categories are most competitive, and which names are emerging.

That intelligence, absorbed in a room with peers, is harder to replicate through trade coverage alone.

The CMA organizers note that the event "provides the ideal setting for an evening tailor-made for sharing insights, networking and building connections."

A brokerage that treats the evening as a strategic exercise, briefing its staff on who else will be in the room and what conversations are worth having, is likely to leave with more than a photograph.
